items.question: How do you think about AI's ability to produce major scientific innovations?
items.object: AI-driven scientific innovation
items.answer: I think a lot of analogies from evolution transfer to scientific research, in the sense that we traverse a tree of different ideas or different experiments, and then in the paper we report one path through that tree. When we run LLMs autonomously, nothing interesting tends to happen. But oftentimes innovation for a specific problem might require first inventing a different problem. Automatically coming up with this reduction or, let's say, this recursive nature of problem solving is something these systems right now don't necessarily have built in intrinsically. Oftentimes it's easier to generate a lot of solutions than to hard verify them. And I think one of the Rubicon moments is when the new transformers architecture or something massive is discovered by AI, and we're all using it.

items.question: What do you see as Shinka Evolve's main contribution to evolutionary search with language models?
items.object: Shinka Evolve's contribution to evolutionary search with language models
items.answer: First off, of course, this was partially inspired by AlphaEvolve. I think it's great work. I know Alex and Mate, and I think they're doing incredible science. One thing that is important about using all of these evolutionary LLM driven methods is sample efficiency. So many of these systems sample, let's say, 1,000 programs for a given task. And what we try to do with Shinka Evolve was essentially cut down costs as well as computation evaluation time by introducing a set of technical innovations to this evolutionary search. And we showed that it's possible with very few program evaluations to basically improve upon, for example, the circle packing canonical result that they showed in their paper. More generally speaking, I think we are right now at an inflection point where these evolutionary driven LLM systems can really revolutionize scientific discovery. And we hope to have made a step forward to making this more democratically accessible. So the code is open source available and, by its sample efficient nature, we hope that many people can interact with the system and can make their own scientific discoveries as well.

items.question: Why do you think open-ended AI discovery needs problems and solutions to evolve together?
items.object: Coevolution of problems and solutions in open-ended AI discovery
items.answer: One thing I find extremely important after having done Shinka Evolve is this problem problem. With all of these systems so far, maybe except for the AI scientist, which we can also talk about, the problem is given. So you have an evaluator, you have a correctness checker, and you sample programs only on that single problem. But oftentimes, innovation for a specific problem might require first inventing a different problem. For example, I think in the matrix multiplication result that the AlphaEvolve people show, you can recursively apply the algorithm to larger matrices, so it's actually an important result. But automatically coming up with this reduction or, let's say, this recursive nature of problem solving is something these systems right now don't necessarily have built in intrinsically. items.question: How do you think the starting solution shapes an LLM-driven optimization system’s ability to discover something new?
items.object: Starting conditions and the tradeoff between novelty and convergence in LLM-driven optimization
items.answer: I think it really kind of also depends on what you give the LLM as a starting point. For example, in Shinka Evolve, from time to time we saw that if you give an initial solution program which is already pretty optimized on the problem at hand, you still kind of get stuck in local optima, where not a lot of novelty is introduced. While if you start off from an impoverished solution, there's much more room for diversity. And I think this is coming back to what I did before in my research, namely meta learning, this classical tradeoff where you can either start out from something very unconstrained, from a very simple solution, and give much more room for the optimization. But this might actually require open endedness and a long time to find a good solution, or you start out from something that is already very constrained by inductive biases, let's say, and then you might be much more efficient in terms of convergence. But you don't have the open ended big novelty benefit from it.

items.question: How do you think about making Shinka Evolve’s LLM-driven program evolution scale more effectively?
items.object: Shinka Evolve’s approach to scaling program evolution with LLMs
items.answer: The way Shinka Evolve, similar to AlphaEvolve, works is you keep an archive, like a database of programs, and then you sample parent programs with a set of inspiration programs. And then you ask an LLM to make an improvement to that program, to provide code edits or rewrite an entire program or potentially even cross over different programs. And then you query the LLM, you get a program out, and you evaluate it on the problem at hand. For example, increasing the sum of the radii of a bunch of circles in a square. You run this each time, collecting evidence from the evaluator, adding it to the database, and then repeating this process. And you don't do this sequentially, but you do this in parallel for many different programs. And each time a program is added, you essentially try to diffuse the knowledge that was collected by that program across the entire database. So one way to think about this is you have a tree, a tree where each node in the tree represents a program, and then you branch off of it based on the parent nodes. And interestingly, these approaches do tend to scale, but ideally can make the scaling at a faster rate. And this is something we tried in Shinka Evolve by doing a bunch of innovations, including model ensembling. So we're not using just Gemini, but we're using basically all frontier model providers and figuring out a smart way how to use each model for a given parent. If you have a certain program, in some situations it might be better to use a GPT model; in other settings it might be better to use a Gemini model. And we introduce an adaptive prioritization scheme that can adapt the evolutionary algorithm on the fly while running the algorithm. And this also comes back to the naming. Shinka Evolve evolve evolve kind of means that this evolutionary algorithm that we apply using LLMs also coevolves at the same time while we optimize the programs.

items.question: Why do you see surrogate problems as valuable for automated discovery?
items.object: Surrogate problems as aids to automated discovery
items.answer: I think one thing that was very interesting about the circle packing problem was that originally we used a formulation where the correctness is checked with a very tiny amount of slack. So the circles could overlap a tiny little bit. And then afterwards we reduced the radii and the solution was exact. This didn't change the score by too much, so it's still state of the art, but it was essentially a proxy problem. We then reran the Shinka Evolve on the exact setting, and we found that it took a little bit longer to actually obtain the same quality of a solution. So I think this already points a little bit in this direction of what I discussed in the beginning: sometimes surrogate problems might actually be extremely valuable in making such discoveries. And having an automated way for designing these surrogate problems in an efficient way might be something really important going forward.

items.answer: One thing we do in Shinka Evolve is we keep essentially a scratch pad. So each program is being summarized. And then from the program summaries, we keep a set of global insights, let's say, that are shared or extracted from these programs. And then based off of the scratch pad, we construct meta recommendations that then become part of the system prompt. That way, you can try to semantically grasp some of the discoveries. items.question: How do you decide which language model to use for proposing program mutations in evolutionary search?
items.object: Language model selection for proposing program mutations in evolutionary search
items.answer: We're using a model ensemble to propose program mutations. And intuitively, one could say the best frontier model on SWE bench is always the best mutation proposal model. But that's actually in practice not always the case. And in general, it's extremely hard in this evolutionary setting to assign clear credit to a single model. So you have, for example, one improvement implemented by GPT 5, and then the next one is implemented by Sonnet 4.5. And it's unclear if the performance gain you get from the second mutation actually originated from GPT 5 collecting the first stepping stone or from Sonnet 4.5. So instead of uniformly sampling models, what we do is we implement this bandit based approach where each model is one arm of a bandit. And then we look at how often this model improved performance of a parent node by creating a mutation. And we then adjust this posterior probability to first explore all arms once, and then change over the course of time in order to prefer models that yielded improvements before for similar nodes.

items.question: How do you make LLM-generated program mutations robust while preserving code essential to evaluation?
items.object: Code markers and rejection sampling for LLM program mutations
items.answer: A program is just a long string. And in order to make sure that certain parts which are essential to the evaluation, for example the imports and so on, are not deleted by the LLM mutations, there are so called markers, which basically state which parts of the code are mutable and evolvable. And it's easy to programmatically make them actually immutable when you get a diff proposal, and these will not be changed. So only the rest of the code snippet will be changed. We implement a type of rejection sampling with reflection approach where if an LLM by chance, for example, tries to mutate this part, it's gonna be rejected and you resample a new proposal. Thereby you can somewhat mitigate certain security or safety problems and get a robust mutation.

items.question: How do you think about the value of using program rewrites and crossover alongside diff-based mutations in evolutionary code search?
items.object: Program-rewriting and crossover mutations in evolutionary code search
items.answer: A small innovation on top of AlphaEvolve, where I believe they only use diff based mutations, is that here we wanted to have more flexibility to entirely rewrite the program, to come up with a completely different stepping stone, if you will. So, again, there you can make parts of the code mutable, but instead of proposing a patch to change certain parts of it, we essentially rewrite the entire program. And this sometimes is helpful. It's not always a clear benefit, but it allows you to get more diversity into the search. So this is one type of mutation next to this diff patch based approach, and the other one is a crossover mutation where we sample not only a single parent program, but two different ones, and we ask the system to make a complementary improvement. And again, on some problems, this is really helpful and on others, it's not. But in general, we found that having a diversity in terms of operators is also helpful in discovering new things.

items.question: What do you see as a major challenge in using language models to discover solutions on people's behalf?
items.object: Automatic verification in language-model-driven discovery
items.answer: I think one of the bigger problems there is this verification aspect to it. Oftentimes it's easier to generate a lot of solutions than to hard verify them. Language models are capable of doing soft verification, looking at code, and latently running a stack trace of execution. But it's not exact. And I think these notions of reward hacking and not doing real discoveries, but shortcutting them, is where we need to put more time and effort into figuring out how to make sure that this actually moves in the right direction. items.question: How do you think AI Scientist v2 better captures the scientific method than v1?
items.object: AI Scientist v2’s approach to the scientific method
items.answer: In v1, we used a template based approach. So we had a base experiment. And then for that base experiment, we asked an LLM to generate ideas with Semantic Scholar calls and literature search, and then it implemented these ideas based on the template. It did code diffs. And then it linearly executed an experiment plan and wrote a paper in the end. And so what could happen was that there was an idea and that idea didn't work out. But then in the end the experiments were still executed linearly when you wrote a paper. And this was already impressive in the sense that it looked very much like science. But if you think about human science and the scientific method, it's much more like tree search, like I said before. You adapt what you're gonna execute next, and you refine based on evidence that you accumulated. This is the notion of falsificationism from Karl Popper, in the sense that we collect evidence for hypotheses and reject others, and we do so in a loop until we want to publish or we find something. And we try to take this notion and directly build it into the agentic scaffolding for the AI Scientist v2. So now it's basically a parallelizable agentic tree search where there's no longer a template experiment needed, but this is drafted up by the LLM itself. And thereby the AI Scientist v2 can be applied to many more settings. At the core is this new agentic tree search paradigm, and then we use a couple of minor technical changes, like using a VLM reviewer for figuring out if captions of a paper are aligned with the figures. We scale this up to many more computational nodes and then write a paper in the end again.
